Quantile Tail Weight Measure

Source: R/quantile_weight.R
quantile_weight.Rd

This function calculates the left quantile weight (LQW) and the right quantile weight (RQW) for a given numeric vector. These weights serve as robust measures of tail heaviness, providing insights into the distribution's behavior in the left and right tails, respectively.

Usage

quantile_weight(
  x,
  p = 0.125,
  q = 0.875,
  drop_na = FALSE,
  drop.na = deprecated()
)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector.

p

A probability between 0 and 0.5 that chooses the quantiles of the left half compared by LQW: \(Q(p/2)\) and \(Q((1-p)/2)\) of the data. A smaller value looks further into the left tail. Default is 0.125.

q

A probability between 0.5 and 1 that chooses the quantiles of the right half compared by RQW: \(Q(1-q/2)\) and \(Q((1+q)/2)\) of the data. A larger value looks further into the right tail. Default is 0.875.

drop_na

Logical value indicating whether to remove missing values (NA). If FALSE (default) and x contains missing values, NA is returned.

drop.na

Use drop_na.

Value

A tibble with two numeric columns:

  • LQW: Left quantile weight.

  • RQW: Right quantile weight.

Details

The left quantile weight (LQW) and the right quantile weight (RQW) are robust measures of tail weight (Brys et al. 2006). They apply the quantile skewness of Hinkley (1975), $$SK(p) = \frac{Q(1-p) + Q(p) - 2Q(0.5)}{Q(1-p) - Q(p)},$$ to each half of the distribution, divided at the median: the left half, whose median is the first quartile \(Q(0.25)\), and the right half, whose median is the third quartile \(Q(0.75)\): $$LQW(p) = -\frac{Q((1-p)/2) + Q(p/2) - 2Q(0.25)}{Q((1-p)/2) - Q(p/2)}$$ $$RQW(q) = \frac{Q((1+q)/2) + Q(1-q/2) - 2Q(0.75)}{Q((1+q)/2) - Q(1-q/2)}$$ where \(Q\) is the quantile function of the data. p and q are probabilities that choose the quantiles compared: LQW compares \(Q(p/2)\) and \(Q((1-p)/2)\), the \(p\) and \(1 - p\) quantiles of the left half, around \(Q(0.25)\); RQW compares \(Q(1-q/2)\) and \(Q((1+q)/2)\), the \(1 - q\) and \(q\) quantiles of the right half, around \(Q(0.75)\). A heavier tail stretches the outer quantile further than the inner one, which gives a larger weight. With \(q = 1 - p\), both weights look equally far into their tails. The defaults, p = 0.125 and q = 0.875, compare \(Q(0.0625)\) and \(Q(0.4375)\) for LQW, and \(Q(0.5625)\) and \(Q(0.9375)\) for RQW.

The breakdown value of LQW is \(p/2\) and that of RQW is \((1 - q)/2\): 6.25% for the defaults, which resist up to 6.25% of outliers in a tail. A smaller p (or a q closer to 1) looks further into the tails, which makes the weights more sensitive to the tail weight but less robust; p = 0.25 and q = 0.75 give a breakdown value of 12.5%, as medcouple_weight().

Interpretation of the quantile weights:

  • At the normal distribution, LQW = RQW = 0.249 with the defaults (0.144 with p = 0.25 and q = 0.75).

  • Larger values indicate heavier tails than the normal distribution, and smaller values lighter tails.

References

  • Brys, G., Hubert, M., and Struyf, A. (2006). Robust measures of tail weight. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 50(3):733-759

  • Hinkley, D.V., (1975). On power transformations to symmetry. Biometrika, 62(1):101–111.

See also

medcouple_weight(), medcouple()

Author

Christian L. Goueguel

Examples

# 10000 values from three symmetric distributions: uniform (light tails),
# normal, and Laplace (double exponential: heavy tails)
set.seed(1)
n <- 10000
tails <- data.frame(
  distribution = factor(rep(c("uniform", "normal", "Laplace"), each = n),
                        levels = c("uniform", "normal", "Laplace")),
  value = c(runif(n, -2, 2), rnorm(n),
            rexp(n) * sample(c(-1, 1), n, replace = TRUE))
)
ggplot2::ggplot(tails, ggplot2::aes(value, fill = distribution)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-5, 5)) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fdb863", "#2166ac", "#b2182b"))


# the weights grow with the tail weight, in both tails: about 0 for the
# uniform distribution, 0.25 for the normal one and 0.43 for the Laplace one
weights <- function(v) c(kurtosis = moments::kurtosis(v), unlist(quantile_weight(v)))
round(t(sapply(split(tails$value, tails$distribution), weights)), 3)
#>         kurtosis   LQW    RQW
#> uniform    1.789 0.032 -0.040
#> normal     2.978 0.255  0.248
#> Laplace    6.103 0.441  0.439

# 1% of outliers: 9900 normal values and 100 near 10. The kurtosis jumps
# from 3 to 25, while the right quantile weight hardly moves and the left
# one does not see the outliers
set.seed(2)
x <- c(rnorm(9900), rnorm(100, mean = 10, sd = 0.5))
group <- rep(c("regular", "outlier"), c(9900, 100))
ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(x, group), ggplot2::aes(x)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(fill = "#2166ac", alpha = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_rug(ggplot2::aes(colour = group)) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(outlier = "#b2182b", regular = "#2166ac"))

round(weights(x), 3)
#> kurtosis      LQW      RQW 
#>   25.304    0.235    0.271 

data(forageLIBS)
# iron contents (mg/kg): a few samples are far above the others
fe <- forageLIBS$Fe[!is.na(forageLIBS$Fe)]
moments::kurtosis(fe)   # classical
#> [1] 25.01662
quantile_weight(fe)     # robust, left and right tails
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>      LQW   RQW
#>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.0174 0.687
